worksheet.title: Move Blocks
worksheet.subtitle: Each block points the way Bit goes
worksheet.learning_goal: I can match a move block to the way it makes Bit go.

parts.title: One block, one way
parts.text: A move block tells Bit ONE way to go. ➡ moves Bit RIGHT. ⬅ moves Bit LEFT. ⬆ moves Bit UP. ⬇ moves Bit DOWN. One block makes one step in one direction.

parts.title: The move blocks
parts.note: Four move blocks. Each arrow points the way Bit will travel.

parts.title: Find UP
parts.prompt: Circle the move block that makes Bit go UP.

parts.title: Find LEFT
parts.prompt: Circle the move block that makes Bit go to the LEFT.

parts.title: An empty block
parts.note: This block has no arrow yet.

parts.title: You try
parts.prompt: Bit wants to go DOWN. Draw the arrow in the empty block that tells Bit to go DOWN. It points ⬇.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Each move block points the way Bit goes. To make Bit move a certain way, you pick the block with that arrow. That is how you tell a computer exactly what to do.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Kindergarten · Intro Block Coding
teacher_guide.title: Move Blocks
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Children learn the move-block vocabulary of block coding: each arrow block makes the character travel in exactly one direction (➡ right, ⬅ left, ⬆ up, ⬇ down). Connecting a symbol to one precise action is the foundation for reading and writing programs in the next sheets.

parts.title: Kindergarten frame (Ontario)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children use directional language and symbols to describe movement.
No reading required of the child: read each prompt aloud; the child circles a block or draws one arrow.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor space to step the directions, or four arrow cards (➡ ⬅ ⬆ ⬇).

parts.title: Run it (about 15 min)
text: 1. MODEL: hold up each move block and act it out with your whole arm — '➡ right… ⬅ left… ⬆ up… ⬇ down.' One block, one way.
2. GUIDED: Exercise 1 — circle the ⬆ block (up). Exercise 2 — circle the ⬅ block (left).
3. YOU TRY: Exercise 3 — children draw a ⬇ arrow in the empty block to make Bit go down.
4. Connect: 'To tell a computer which way to go, you give it the block with that arrow.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — UP is the ⬆ block (the arrow points up).
Ex 2 — LEFT is the ⬅ block (the arrow points left).
Ex 3 — DOWN is the ⬇ block: the child draws an arrow pointing straight down in the empty block.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common mix-up: left ⬅ vs right ➡. Anchor to the child's own hands ('this is your LEFT hand') before they circle.
Simplify: do the arm movement together first, then point to the matching block.
Extend: call a direction and have the child point to the matching block as fast as they can.
Movement option: tape the four arrow cards to walls; call a direction, children walk that way.

parts.title: Success looks like
parts.text: The child circles the up and left blocks correctly and draws a downward arrow for 'down', showing each block stands for one specific direction.
